This kind of hurt is not just sadness. It carries a very specific flavour: it is the pain that comes from feeling wronged by another person. It almost always involves a relationship — a friend, a parent, a partner, a colleague. Hurt in this sense says: "What you did (or said) damaged me."

"She tried to smile, but the hurt in her eyes was impossible to hide."
"He carried the hurt of his father's rejection for many years."
"I could hear the hurt in her voice when she spoke about it."

Notice how in these examples, "hurt" is not just pain in general — it is personal, relational, and directed. Someone caused it.

2. Physical Injury or Pain (Less Common)

As a noun, "hurt" can also refer to a physical injury or the physical sensation of pain. However, this use is less common in modern everyday English. People are far more likely to say "injury," "pain," or "wound" when talking about the body. The noun "hurt" in a physical sense appears more often in older literature, or in informal speech.

"He walked with a slight limp, trying to shake off the hurt in his ankle."
"The child cried, clutching the hurt on her arm."

You will understand this use if you encounter it, but you are unlikely to need to produce it yourself very often.

3. Harm or Damage (Formal / Old-Fashioned)

In a more formal or slightly old-fashioned register, "hurt" as a noun can mean harm or damage — the idea that something caused a negative effect on a person, group, or situation.

"No hurt was intended by his words."
"It does no hurt to ask."
"The scandal caused lasting hurt to the organisation's reputation."

In this sense, it is close in meaning to the words "harm" or "damage." You will mostly see this in formal writing or in classic literature.

This is a subtle but important point.

When "hurt" refers to emotional pain as a general feeling, it is uncountable — you cannot put "a" in front of it or make it plural.

✅ "There was so much hurt between them."
❌ "There was so much hurts between them."

However, when "hurt" refers to specific, individual experiences of emotional pain — particular moments or events that wounded someone — it can be used as a countable noun and made plural.

✅ "She had to let go of all the old hurts from her childhood."
✅ "Years of small hurts had slowly destroyed their friendship."

In this plural form, "hurts" means individual instances of being emotionally wounded — specific memories or events that left a mark.
The Feeling of Hurt — Up Close

To really understand this word, it helps to understand what emotional "hurt" feels like as an experience, because the word is used to capture something very precise.

Hurt is the pain that sits between sadness and anger. When you feel hurt, you feel:

  • Wounded — as if something inside you has been cut or bruised
  • Disappointed — someone or something did not treat you the way you deserved or expected
  • Vulnerable — your trust, love, or openness was not respected

Hurt is different from anger (which is outward and reactive), different from grief (which is specifically about loss, especially death), and different from general sadness (which does not require another person to have caused it). Hurt is almost always the result of what someone else did or said to you.

This is why we often talk about hurt using the language of wounds and medicine:

  • "The hurt ran deep." (It was a serious wound.)
  • "Old hurts that never healed." (Emotional scars from the past.)
  • "She nursed her hurt in silence." (She quietly dwelt on her pain.)
  • "It took years to get past the hurt." (To recover from the emotional injury.)

Here are natural, everyday ways "hurt" appears as a noun, so you can recognise and use them confidently:

  • "the hurt in someone's eyes/voice" — visible or audible emotional pain
    "I could see the hurt in his eyes."*
  • "feel the hurt" — to experience emotional pain
    "She didn't show it, but she felt the hurt deeply."*
  • "hide the hurt" — to conceal your emotional pain from others
    "He was always good at hiding the hurt."*
  • "cause hurt" — to wound someone emotionally
    "She never meant to cause him any hurt."*
  • "old hurts" — emotional wounds from the past
    "They had to talk through a lot of old hurts before they could move on."*
  • "no hurt intended / no hurt meant" — no harm or offence was meant
    "Please don't take it the wrong way — no hurt was intended."*
  • "deep hurt" — strong, serious emotional pain
    "There was a deep hurt inside her that she had never talked about."*

WordWhat makes it different

Pain is broader and more physical. You can have pain in your knee, your head, your stomach. "Hurt" (as a noun) is more personal and more emotional in modern usage.

Grief is specifically the pain of loss — usually the death of someone you love, or the end of something deeply important. Hurt is more general and relational.

Anguish is more intense and overwhelming than hurt — it implies extreme suffering, often physical or desperate. Hurt is quieter and more personal.

Wound (as a noun) is mostly physical. But when used metaphorically — "the wounds of the past" — it overlaps very closely with "hurt."

Offence is specifically the feeling that someone has violated a rule of respect or decency. Hurt is the pain that often results from being offended. They are related, but hurt is the feeling; offence is more about the act.

If you ever forget everything else, remember this:

Hurt (noun) = the pain — especially emotional pain — that results from being wounded by what someone said or did.

It is the quiet ache in your chest when a friend betrays you, the sting in your heart when someone dismisses you, the lasting bruise left by years of unkindness. It is personal, it is real, and it almost always involves another person.
7896: Hurt means to cause pain or damage, or to feel pain or damage. The pain can be in your body, in your emotions, or in a situation. This single word covers all of these, which is what makes it so powerful and widely used.

1. To Cause Physical Pain to Someone or Something

This is when an action produces pain in a person's body — yours or someone else's.

  • The hot pan hurt her hand when she touched it.
  • Stop it! You're hurting me!
  • He fell off his bike and hurt his knee.

Here, something is actively causing physical pain. There is a cause (the pan, "you", the fall) and a victim (her hand, me, his knee).

2. To Feel Physical Pain (in a part of your body)

This is when a part of your body sends you a signal of pain. You are not necessarily doing anything — the pain is just there.

  • My back hurts.
  • Does your tooth still hurt?
  • My legs hurt after the long run.

Notice here that the body part is the subject of the sentence. The body part is "doing" the hurting — meaning it is the source of the pain you feel. This is one of the most common everyday uses of the word.

3. To Cause Emotional Pain

Hurt is not only about the body. It is very commonly used for emotional or psychological pain — the kind of pain you feel in your heart, not your body.

  • His harsh words really hurt her.
  • It hurt me deeply when she didn't come to my wedding.
  • You hurt his feelings when you laughed at his idea.

This emotional sense is used constantly in everyday life. When someone says or does something unkind, dismissive, or unfair, and it makes you feel sad, rejected, or wounded inside — that is hurt.

4. To Feel Emotional Pain

Just as a body part can "hurt," a person can "be hurting" emotionally — meaning they are going through deep sadness, grief, or emotional suffering.

  • She is really hurting after the breakup.
  • I could see he was hurting, even though he pretended to be fine.
  • It's okay to admit that you're hurting.

This use is slightly softer and more continuous — it describes an ongoing emotional state rather than a single moment.

5. To Harm, Damage, or Weaken Something

This meaning goes beyond personal pain. Here, hurt means to damage, weaken, or have a bad effect on something — a situation, a cause, a reputation, a business, etc.

  • The bad reviews hurt the restaurant's business.
  • Missing so many classes will hurt your grades.
  • The scandal hurt the politician's career.
  • Drought hurt the wheat crops this year.

In this sense, no one necessarily feels pain directly — but something is made worse, weaker, or less effective because of something else.
One Crucial Grammar Point: Hurt Never Changes

Hurt is an irregular verb. This means its form stays exactly the same in the past and past participle — you never say "hurted."

TenseForm
Presenthurt
Pasthurt
Past participlehurt
  • Present: "This hurts."
  • Past: "That hurt."
  • Past participle (with have/has/had): "I have hurt my shoulder before."

All three are simply hurt. Never "hurted." This is a common mistake to avoid.
Transitive vs. Intransitive (Does it need an object?)

Hurt can work both ways — with or without a direct object.

With an object (transitive): Something or someone hurts something or someone else.

  • The punch hurt him. (him = the object receiving the hurt)

Without an object (intransitive): Something simply hurts, all on its own.

  • My shoulder hurts. (no object — the shoulder is just in pain)

Both are perfectly correct. Context tells you which meaning is intended.

Hurt can range from very mild to very severe, and you can show this with adverbs or other words around it.

  • Mild: My eyes hurt a little from staring at the screen.
  • Moderate: The injection hurt quite a bit.
  • Severe: The injury hurt terribly — she could barely walk.

The word itself is neutral in intensity. The words around it carry the degree.

"It wouldn't hurt to..."
This means: it would be a good idea, or at least harmless, to do something.

  • It wouldn't hurt to double-check your work before submitting it.
  • It wouldn't hurt him to say thank you once in a while.

This is a soft way of suggesting something without being forceful.

"Hurt someone's feelings"
To make someone feel emotionally wounded, sad, or disrespected.

  • I didn't mean to hurt your feelings — I was just being honest.

"What hurts the most is..."
Used to point out the most painful part of a situation — usually emotionally.

  • What hurt the most was that she never even apologized.

"Hurt pride"
When someone's sense of self-worth or dignity is wounded.

  • He refused help out of hurt pride — he didn't want to seem weak.

It helps to know what hurt is not, so you don't confuse it with similar words.

  • Hurt ≠ Kill or Destroy. Hurt implies pain or damage, but not complete destruction. If something is hurt, it still exists — it is just damaged or in pain.
  • Hurt ≠ Ache. Ache is a specific type of physical pain — dull, continuous, and steady (like a headache or a toothache). Hurt is broader and more general. All aches hurt, but not all hurt is an ache.
  • Hurt ≠ Insult. To insult someone is to say something disrespectful. To hurt someone (emotionally) is the result that an insult might cause. You can hurt someone without insulting them — for example, by ignoring them or breaking a promise.

The word hurt is essentially about pain and damage in their many forms — physical, emotional, and situational. What makes it unique is its flexibility: the same word covers the act of causing pain, the experience of feeling pain, and the effect of weakening or damaging something. Whether your knee hurts, someone's words hurt you, or a bad decision hurts your chances — the word "hurt" is doing its job across all of it.
7897:
If something is hurtful, it causes emotional pain to someone. It makes a person feel sad, upset, wounded, or offended. Think of it this way — just as a sharp knife can hurt your body, a hurtful word, action, or behavior can hurt your feelings deeply.

The word almost always describes emotional or psychological pain, not physical pain. When someone says "That was hurtful," they mean "That damaged my feelings."

The word "hurtful" is used to describe things — not people directly. Specifically, it most commonly describes:

Words and speech — A comment, remark, joke, or criticism can be hurtful if it wounds someone's feelings. "She made a hurtful comment about his weight."

Actions and behavior — What someone does (or fails to do) can also be hurtful. "Being ignored by your friends is a deeply hurtful experience."

Situations and events — Even a circumstance or experience can be hurtful. "Losing the job he loved was hurtful to his sense of self-worth."
Does It Have to Be Intentional?

This is one of the most important things to understand about "hurtful" — no, it does not have to be intentional. Something can be hurtful even when no harm was meant at all.

For example: Imagine someone says to their friend, "You look tired today" — they might just be expressing concern, but the friend might find it hurtful because it made them feel unattractive. The speaker didn't mean to cause pain, but the effect was still hurtful.

This is what separates "hurtful" from a word like "cruel." Cruelty almost always involves a deliberate wish to cause pain. Hurtfulness is about the effect — whether pain was caused — regardless of the intention behind it.

"Hurtful" sits in the mild to moderate range of emotional pain — but it can be made stronger with words placed before it:

  • "a slightly hurtful remark" → a mild sting
  • "a deeply hurtful betrayal" → serious emotional wound
  • "a particularly hurtful thing to say" → emphasizing how much it stings in context

It is not as extreme as "devastating" or "traumatizing," but it is stronger than something merely "unpleasant" or "awkward."

"Hurtful" is almost always used from the perspective of the person who feels the pain — or from someone observing and sympathizing with them. It is a word that validates emotional experience. When you call something hurtful, you are essentially saying: "This caused real emotional damage, and that matters."

This makes it a powerful word in emotional conversations, apologies, and confrontations.

• It is not the same as "harmful", which is broader and often refers to physical, social, or long-term damage (e.g., "Smoking is harmful to your health"). Hurtful is almost exclusively emotional.
  • It is not the same as "offensive", which focuses more on violating social, cultural, or moral standards — something offensive might not be personally hurtful, and something hurtful might not technically be offensive to others.
  • It is not the same as "mean", which describes the character or attitude behind an action. Someone can say something hurtful without being a mean person.

Words with similar meaning: wounding, cutting, unkind, upsetting, distressing, painful (emotionally), cruel (stronger)

Words with opposite meaning: kind, gentle, caring, comforting, considerate, supportive, uplifting

• "His words were so hurtful that she couldn't stop thinking about them for days."
  • "I didn't mean it that way — I'm sorry if what I said came across as hurtful."
  • "It's hurtful when people dismiss your feelings without listening."
  • "Spreading rumors about someone is one of the most hurtful things you can do."
  • "She found his silence more hurtful than any argument could have been."
If you ever need to remember this word in its simplest form: Hurtful means "causing emotional pain to someone," whether that pain was intended or not.
7898:
To hurtle means to move at great speed in a way that feels forceful, uncontrolled, or dangerously unstoppable.

It is not just about being fast. It is about being powerfully, recklessly fast — the kind of speed that feels like it has a life of its own, where stopping or slowing down seems almost impossible.

Think of a massive boulder rolling down a steep hill, crushing everything in its path. Or a racing car that has lost its brakes. That combination of high speed + raw force + lack of control is the heart of "hurtle."

Every time you use this word, it carries two qualities together:

1. Great speed — not a gentle trot or a quick jog. We're talking about dramatic, alarming speed.

2. A sense of force or being out of control — the movement feels heavy, unstoppable, or reckless. There is momentum behind it that is hard to fight.

Remove either of these and "hurtle" starts to feel like the wrong word. A feather drifting quickly in the wind does not "hurtle" — it is too light and gentle. A bulldozer moving slowly does not "hurtle" — it lacks the speed. But a meteor tearing through the atmosphere? That hurtles.

1. Something moves very fast on its own (most common use)

This is the everyday use of the word. A person, vehicle, or object moves at frightening speed.

  • The train hurtled through the tunnel, rattling the windows of every building it passed.
  • She lost her grip on the handlebars and hurtled down the hill on her bicycle.
  • The asteroid hurtled through space on a collision course with Earth.
  • The rollercoaster hurtled around the bend so fast that passengers screamed.

Notice in all these examples, the movement feels dangerous, dramatic, or at least thrillingly fast. There is a sense that the thing moving is not fully in control of itself.

2. Something is thrown or propelled with great force (less common, but correct)

Here, one thing causes another thing to move with violent force. This use is rarer in modern everyday English, but it is perfectly correct.

  • The explosion hurtled chunks of rock across the street.
  • The impact hurtled the driver forward into the windshield.

In these sentences, "hurtle" works like "fling" or "hurl" — but with extra emphasis on the sheer force and speed of what is being sent flying.

3. Figurative use (for situations, not just physical movement)

"Hurtle" can describe abstract things moving rapidly toward a result — usually a bad or dramatic one.

  • The country was hurtling toward a political crisis.
  • His health was hurtling downward despite the treatments.
  • The company hurtled toward bankruptcy after a string of poor decisions.

In these cases, the word still carries its core feeling: things are moving fast, there is powerful momentum behind them, and it is very hard to stop what is happening.
What Makes "Hurtle" Different from Similar Words

Many words describe fast movement, so understanding what makes "hurtle" specifically "hurtle" is important.

  • Rush — fast, but gentle and controlled by comparison. People rush to catch a bus. They hurtle off a cliff.
  • Zoom — fast and fun. Playful, light, often used for small things (a toy car zooms). "Hurtle" is heavier and more serious.
  • Dart — fast and sudden, but small and nimble (a fish darts, a mouse darts). "Hurtle" implies something with weight and momentum behind it.
  • Race — suggests competition or deliberate speed. You can race something on purpose. Hurtling often feels beyond your choice or control.
  • Plummet — only downward (a bird plummets, stocks plummet). "Hurtle" can be in any direction: sideways, downward, forward.
  • Fly — broad and versatile. Flying can be graceful and controlled. Hurtling rarely is.

The clearest way to feel the difference: if you can picture someone calmly in control of the movement, "hurtle" is probably wrong. Hurtle implies the speed has taken over.

"Hurtle" is a vivid, dramatic word. Writers choose it deliberately when they want you to feel the danger and power of fast movement — not just understand it intellectually.

When you read that something hurtled, your brain should picture something massive and fast that you would not want to be in front of. It creates a sense of urgency and alarm.

Compare these two sentences:

  • The car moved quickly down the road. (neutral, flat)
  • The car hurtled down the road. (immediate, alarming — you feel the danger)

Same basic fact. Completely different feeling.

Avoid "hurtle" when:

  • The movement is light, delicate, or graceful (a butterfly, a feather, a dancer)
  • The movement is slow or moderate, no matter how forceful
  • The thing is tiny and carries no real weight or momentum
  • The movement is calm and fully in control (a pilot flying smoothly)

Hurtle = move very fast + with force or lack of control

It is a dramatic word for dramatic movement — the kind that makes your heart race just to watch. Use it for speeding trains, falling boulders, crashing vehicles, and any situation (real or figurative) where powerful momentum is carrying something forward at alarming speed.
7899:
A husband is a man who is married to someone. He is one half of a married couple — specifically, the male half.

When a man gets married, he becomes a husband. When you say "my husband," you mean the man you are married to.

Marriage is a formal union between two people — recognized legally, socially, or both. In that union:

  • The male partner is the husband
  • The female partner is the wife
  • Either partner can also be called a spouse (a gender-neutral word for both)

"Husband" only describes a man in relation to the person he is married to. He holds this title because of the marriage. If the marriage ends, the title changes — he becomes an ex-husband (after a divorce) or a widower (after his spouse dies).
In a marriage between two men, both partners are husbands. So a man can absolutely have a husband. This is correct, standard usage.
A person can have more than one husband — either one after another (through remarriage) or, in certain cultures that permit it, at the same time.

You use "husband" when talking about your spouse to someone else:

  • "My husband is a teacher."
  • "Her husband arrived late."
  • "She introduced me to her husband."

You would not normally address your spouse directly as "husband" — you'd use his name or a term like "dear" or "honey."

The phrase husband and wife simply means a married couple:

  • "They have been husband and wife for fifteen years."

The word appears in both everyday speech and in formal, legal documents — marriage certificates, court records, official forms. In more neutral or modern contexts, people sometimes prefer partner or spouse instead, but husband remains the most common and direct word for a married man.

Historically, in many cultures, the husband was expected to be the head of the household — the main earner and decision-maker. These expectations have shifted significantly. Today, what a husband does within a marriage is shaped by the couple themselves, not by a fixed universal rule.

WordMeaning
WifeThe female partner in a marriage
SpouseEither partner in a marriage (gender-neutral)
PartnerAn informal or neutral term for a spouse
Ex-husbandA man you were previously married to (after divorce)
WidowerA man whose spouse has died
In a sentence — the simplest possible summary:
A husband is a man who is married. He is married to his spouse, who may be called his wife or, in a same-sex marriage, his husband.
